## door v0.1.5 — hardware-key two-factor login (FIDO2/U2F)

door now supports a **YubiKey (or any FIDO2/U2F authenticator) as a second
factor**: password **and** a touch to log in. Because the daemon and wire
protocol were already built for multi-round PAM conversations, this required
**no change to the privileged core** — the trust boundary is untouched. The
FIDO2 exchange runs inside the privileged daemon (talking to the key as root
during authentication); the unprivileged greeter only shows the touch cue and
never sees the key or its secret.

### Added
- **FIDO2/U2F 2FA**, policy-neutral. door drives whatever PAM stack you present,
  so you add one `pam_u2f` line to your login stack and door runs it — see the
  new **[docs/yubikey.md](https://github.com/satorisage/door/blob/master/docs/yubikey.md)**
  setup guide (with a prominent lockout-avoidance section).
- **Greeter multi-prompt UI.** The greeter now renders an *arbitrary* PAM
  prompt, not just a pre-typed password: any prompt it can't pre-answer (a FIDO2
  PIN, a second typed factor, a passwordless first prompt) appears as a focused,
  masked-if-secret field whose reply is moved straight into a zeroizing buffer.
- **Distinct touch cue.** One-way "touch your key" messages now render as a
  distinct pulsing indicator instead of a plain status line.
- **Passwordless + FIDO2-PIN** is supported (`sufficient pam_u2f … pinverification=1`)
  for those who want the key to replace the password; the 2FA default is
  recommended.
- **`pam-u2f` optional dependency** for the above.

### Security
- No TCB / privilege-boundary change — the only code touched is the unprivileged,
  pre-auth greeter UI. Threat model documented alongside the auth-path model.
- Yubico OTP / YubiCloud is intentionally **not** supported: it requires network
  validation, and door's "no network, ever" constraint forbids it. FIDO2/U2F is
  fully offline.

### Notes
- The 2FA auth path is validated on real hardware (a console login through the
  same `system-login` stack door authenticates against).
- Reversible by design: keep a backup key and a password fallback so a lost key
  never locks you out — the guide walks through it.
